try hard not think about the trauma

I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

When I remember the event I feel intense shame

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, 'institutional failure' and especially 'betrayal by someone trusted' are hard to reconcile unless the crash involved unusual interpersonal circumstances not reflected anywhere else in the profile. The rest of the profile centers on fear/startle/intrusive sensory recall, which fits an accident trauma; these appraisal items instead imply an interpersonal or systemic-trauma narrative.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: 'Guilt on recall' can occur after accidents, but in this profile it sits awkwardly with the chosen appraisal set: the appraisals focus on betrayal/institutional failure rather than self-blame or responsibility. That makes the guilt theme insufficiently supported across nodes for a coherent cognitive formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the appraisal 'I was betrayed by someone I trusted' is hard to reconcile unless the crash specifically involved a trusted driver or intentional wrongdoing, which is not otherwise reflected anywhere else in the profile. As presented, it introduces a different interpersonal-trauma theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within Negative Appraisals, 'Betrayal' and 'Self-Blame' can sometimes coexist, but in this profile they point to different causal narratives for the trauma (trusted other's betrayal vs one's own actions causing the event) without any supporting context. That makes the appraisal set clinically hard to unify around a single MVC trauma narrative.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me
issues.explanation: The profile contains a hard-to-reconcile blame pattern: strong self-blame and guilt are paired with other-blame rumination as a core maladaptive strategy. Mixed blame can occur, but this combination is the main internal inconsistency in the selected items because the appraisals and memory items point toward inward blame, while the strategy item points toward sustained outward blame.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Within the cognitive formulation, Maladaptive Strategies links most strongly to Negative Appraisals, so the strategy content should fit the appraisal style. Here the appraisal style is dominated by self-blame, helplessness, and permanent emotional damage, making other-blame rumination the least coherent strategy item.

issues.item: Memory: Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, guilt on recall is plausible, especially with self-blame, so it is not problematic by itself. The concern is specifically its combination with persistent other-blame rumination, which pulls the profile toward a different blame direction than the rest of the formulation.

vignette: The gravel truck's brakes had failed on the winding coastal highway, and Javier remembered the sickening lurch as his sedan rolled three times. Metal screamed against asphalt, glass shattered inward like cold rain, and the steering column crushed against his chest. He lay trapped in the overturned cabin, breathing in the sharp tang of coolant and blood, while the driver's anguished cries slowly faded into silence. In the weeks that followed, Javier found himself completely unable to put the event into words. The horror remained a heavy, wordless weight, surfacing not as a coherent story but as a sudden, high-pitched whine of tearing metal echoing in his head. Each time that auditory fragment surfaced, a wave of intense shame washed over him, leaving him staring at his hands as if they belonged to someone else. The relentless quality of those intrusions quickly forged new habits. Javier had come to believe that fighting the memories would only make them stronger, so he deliberately tried to leave his body, blanking out his mind the moment the metal-screeching started. He told himself that staying up until very late would keep the trauma at bay, and he forced himself to suppress thoughts of the crash, pushing his attention onto mundane studio tasks until his eyes burned with exhaustion. Paradoxically, the longer he resisted the experience, the more fragmented it became. His habit of suppressing thoughts only served to fracture the memory further, ensuring it would surface later as unprocessable noise rather than lived narrative. This relentless mental exhaustion eroded his sense of self, convincing him that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again and that the collision had occurred simply because he was the sort of man who brought ruin upon himself. That deepening conviction kept his nervous system permanently on high alert. Because he was certain he could not stop bad things from happening, his body prepared for the next disaster before it even arrived. He started scanning for exits the moment he stepped into any room, his eyes darting toward windows and doors instead of the faces of his students. When a colleague reached to tap his shoulder during rehearsal, Javier reacted with alarm, his body flinching as if another collision were imminent. The constant hypervigilance, in turn, fed directly back into his psychological landscape. The sustained fear and scanning never gave his mind a moment to rest, which meant the traumatic fragments were never properly processed and kept returning with fresh intensity. Worse, the relentless negative emotions his own body produced began to confirm his worst fears, cementing his belief that he was fundamentally powerless and that his emotional capacity was permanently broken. These cycles finally caught up with his livelihood. Javier had spent thirty years choreographing and teaching Latin dance, but the studio now felt like a gauntlet. He could not allow his dancers to make contact during lifts, nor could he stand in the center of a packed room without fixating on the double doors behind him. Elena watched as her husband withdrew into a quiet, exhausted version of himself, skipping meals and avoiding the very profession that had defined his life. He finally sought help not because the memories had lessened, but because the weight of waiting for the next disaster had made it impossible to teach, to love, or to simply breathe. He was ready to stop running from the crash, hoping someone could show him how to feel like himself again without feeling the need to leave his body or stay awake until dawn.
